title: Gamma API: How It Works, Pricing and Credits (2026)
summary: Gamma API generates content asynchronously with tiered pricing and documented rate limits. Understand error responses and account tiers to estimate costs.
body_markdown:
## Handling common Gamma API errors


You will mostly meet four classes of Gamma API error: rejected credentials, an empty credit balance, rate limiting, and generations that run long or fail. Only the first is fixed by changing the request itself; the rest are handled by the code around it.


Retrying is correct for only some of these. The rest need a person or a changed input, and each class has its own cause and handling.


When the API key is missing, revoked or belongs to a different workspace than you assumed, that is an auth failure; don't retry, and alert the key's owner.


Insufficient credits means the workspace balance can't cover the generation; check the balance before queuing work and stop the queue rather than retrying.


Too many requests, or too many generations running at once, show up as a 429 or` workspace_concurrency_limit_exceeded` ; back off and retry. Bad input means the request body fails validation; fix the payload, because retries repeat the same failure.


A failed or slow generation means the job started but didn't complete in a reasonable time; poll within a bound, then log and escalate.


### Gamma API authentication and credit errors


Before anything else, establish who owns the key. An authentication failure usually means the key was rotated, revoked or created by someone who has since left, so the handling is to stop and notify the owner, not to retry.


From the caller's side, a credit failure looks similar, but the cause is different: the workspace balance, not the credential.


Check the balance before a batch starts, and halt the batch on the first credit error. Retrying a create request can spend credits twice, and it also fills your logs and hides the real problem.


When a 429 or a` workspace_concurrency_limit_exceeded` response comes back, you're sending work faster than the workspace allows. Retry with exponential backoff and some randomness, and cap the number of attempts.


The concurrency error also tells you something specific: generations are still in flight, so lowering your parallelism fixes it more reliably than waiting longer.


### Slow or failed generations


Poll with a ceiling on both interval growth and total wait time. When the ceiling is reached, stop and record the generation ID instead of polling forever.


If you receive results by webhook, keep the same ceiling as a fallback timer, because a missed callback otherwise looks identical to a slow job. Log every generation ID, since support and your own audit trail both depend on it.


**A retried create request can start a second generation and spend credits twice.** Before retrying a create call that timed out, look up whether a generation already exists for that work item, using the ID you logged or a key you store against the item.


Retry only when none is found. Space out your polling requests, since polling counts against your rate allowance.
